title: Tim Hockin - Is Kubernetes Good for Agents? Infrastructure Solutions for Agent Shaped Problems

segments.text: TIM HOCKIN: Thank you all for coming out today.
I didn't realize this conference was on a weekend
when I signed up for it, so I really
appreciate you all coming out instead of getting a day off
of work.
My name is Tim.
You may be familiar with some of my previous projects,
Kubernetes.
If so, I apologize in advance.
Given my background, I tend to look at this agentic AI problem
as an infrastructure problem.
I see it from the bottom up.
The customers that I talk with come to me,
and they say, we've got these agents,
and your explanations of the breadth of agents
is exactly on point.
There's a million kinds of agents,
but they all come to us with a similar problems,
saying we need to run them.
We need to run a lot of them.
We need the efficiencies that we're not getting.
Agent's agentic workloads are very
different from traditional applications, which is, really,
it's caused people to ask, whether Kubernetes
is the right platform to run these things.
It warms my heart to see Kubernetes mentioned
on other people's slides, but I think it's a fair question.
And so given this audience, I'm not
going to go too deeply into how agents are different.
I'll touch on it just a little bit.
I apologize for racing through this material.
I'm happy to do it again in the halls
or talk after we're here for the next two days.
So let's look at a couple of the things that
make agents interesting.
Agents are very bursty.
They tend to work in very short spurts,
and then go idle for a long time, minutes,
hours, even days, weeks at a time.
This means a lot of idle resources,
if you approach it naively.
Agent workloads, generally untrusted.
I think it's a pretty well understood at this point.
Because of that, they have to run in sandboxes,
and we're always looking at new kinds of sandboxing.
And they have to run single tenant,
because you can't share a sandbox.
That would defeat the purpose.
And that means we miss out on a ton of opportunities
for optimizations, specifically the amortization of overheads.
And lastly, they tend to have humans
in the loop, which makes them very sensitive to the perceived
latency of these systems.
Taken together, this makes it problematic to run them
on Kubernetes.
Kubernetes was built for things that run for a long time
and tend to be scale out horizontally scalable,
and you can amortize your costs.
So before jumping to a solution, I'm
going to touch on the state of the art, what we've observed
at Google and in the Kubernetes world, of how people tend
to run agents on Kubernetes.
And there's really only two patterns with a few variations.
So first is the obvious way.
So, Kubernetes has this idea of a runtime class, which
lets you define a sandbox.
And the default runtime class is a docker-style container,
an OCI container.
But we also have runtime classes for gVisor and for microVMs.
And it is an extension point for Kubernetes,
so people can do interesting research around that.
Some event causes the need for a new instance of an agent.
So for example, a user starts a chat session.
This, obviously, requires instantiating their agent,
a special dedicated single tenant instance just for them.
And each of those runs inside of an agent a sandbox pod.
Now, there's some cost.
Starting up a pod on Kubernetes is not the thing
that Kubernetes does the fastest.
It's not optimized for that.
It's not built for that.
It's fast, seconds, usually, but that's not fast enough.
And so depending on what that agent does at startup,
it could take a long time.
And we've seen agents that load runtime environments that can
take 10s or 15 seconds or more, browsers, all sorts of things.
Eventually, that pod becomes ready,
and the user can chat with it, and they send their message
to the pod, and it comes back, and one turn is done.
And now, what?
So because pod startup isn't free, what people tend to do
is they wait for another event.
And how long should they wait?
Well, that really depends on what your agent is doing
and what the startup cost was.
And you have to do some math, and it's
different for everybody.
We've seen this range from tens of seconds at the low end,
to tens of minutes at the high end.
And during those tens of minutes,
your agent is sitting there, consuming resources that
can't be used by anybody else.
And of course, this might happen multiple times.
At 9 minutes and 59 seconds, the next turn might happen,
and you start the whole process over again.
So, eventually, you get a timeout, and you're deemed idle,
and either you're discarded entirely,
or we save your state, somehow.
And then we terminate the pod, right?
This is the standard Kubernetes lifecycle.
Now, keep in mind, this is happening
for every instance of every agent,
for every user that is happening on your systems.
There are tricks we can play with warm pools,
and there's tricks we can play with suspend and resume.
But Kubernetes doesn't support those things natively.
And so you're working around the system,
and it's difficult to justify at this scale.
The second approach is for people
to build a DIY system on top of Kubernetes.
Basically, this looks like a giant workload per machine.
Inside that workload is a manager application.
A bespoke control plane is responsible for scheduling
things into those that mega sandbox.
The manager manages the life cycle.
Everything's opaque.
Kubernetes doesn't know what it's doing.
You end up reinventing large parts of Kubernetes.
It's fairly complicated to build.
It can be very efficient.
It's difficult to operate for smaller companies, especially
startups.
Now, I'm a huge fan of open source.
Maybe you can tell because I work in Kubernetes
for the last 12 years.
I have a deeply-held belief that when it comes to infrastructure,
open always wins.
And so earlier this year, we set out
to build something new, that takes the best parts of both
of these models, leverages Kubernetes where it can,
because almost everybody has some Kubernetes in their fleet,
and builds new components where we have to.
Now, I'm not going to pretend that we've
discovered anything new.
We have not done any Earth-shaking research here.
What we've done is take some of the best ideas from all
of our customers and our users, and tried
to glue them together into a way that everybody can use.
In the same way that you put Kubernetes up
on the slides as the middle box, I
would like to fill in the right-hand second box for you.
So Agent Substrate-- and thank you for mentioning it--
is a project that we began earlier this year
and have open sourced it.
You can go to this URL.
It'll take you to our GitHub.
From a very high level, the model is pretty straightforward.
We don't want idle resources.
We want to use suspend and resume
and cloud storage to multiplex agents onto pre-warmed runners,
and aggressively suspend and resume agents
to take those 10 seconds to 10 minutes of idle,
and drive it down to a single second, or even less.
So let's talk about the goals.
We're Google, so we tend to see things from the large scale
point of view.
We're shooting for very large deployments.
We're looking at billions of sessions under management.
We're looking at tens of thousands
of activations per second.
And we're looking at driving the wake up
time down into the low three-digit milliseconds.
Quickly, I'll introduce some terms.
We have an actor, which is a stand-in term for agent
or sandbox or thing that acts like an agent.
We have an actor template.
If an actor is a cookie, the actor template
is the cookie cutter.
It includes details what kind of sandbox tech.
Is it gVisor, a microVM.
Notably, there can be many different templates
inside of a single Substrate.
We
Have a worker, which is usually a pod,
running in a Kubernetes cluster.
This is the thing that actually consumes resources.
It waits for an assignment of an actor,
and then it runs that actor.
It can run many of them in serial,
and a cluster can have many workers.
And then Atelet is our per node manager
for all of the workers on that node.
We need this for reasons around networking.
And then lastly, Atenet is our enlightened proxy,
which will trigger wakeups on receipt of traffic.
Let's see how those fit together.
Start with a Kubernetes cluster.
Any modern cluster should work.
We support running in time, so you can run it on your laptop.
The cluster admin deploys an instance
of Agent Substrate, which includes an API
server and a storage layer, a controller, which synchronizes
data in and out of Kubernetes.
One or more worker pools, which create deployments,
which create pods to run your workloads in,
Atelets to manage all those workers.
The Atenet net proxy, which knows
how to pass traffic from the outside world
to the inside world.
And then the Substrate admin can create one or more actor
templates, and the controller sees these
and does some prep work.
Specifically, it spins the actor template up,
takes a snapshot of it.
We call it a golden snapshot, stores that somewhere,
so we can use it later.
Now, shifting view quickly to the substrate layer,
which sits on top of all this--
I'll warn you, some of this is aspirational.
We're still working on it.
We have our API server, router, and workers.
Someone, a higher order system, creates
an actor from that template, for example, the same chat agent.
The chat app does whatever front end
work it needs to do, authorize it, whatever, and then it
creates an actor.
Note, creating an actor doesn't run
the actor in this hypothetical app, the user talks first.
So the user sends a prompt, which is received and routed
to the Atenet proxy.
It wakes up the actor, assigns it to a worker
by sending a message through the router,
and then talks to the worker on a private connection.
Since this is a new actor, it wakes it up
from the Golden snapshot.
The Atenet proxy forwards the message
on to the now-running actor.
And the cool part this happens in a couple 100 milliseconds,
and we're working on that optimization, still.
As soon as that turn is done, the actor is probably idle,
so we can tell it to go back to sleep and suspend it.
We call it pause.
It can be pause, take the snapshot,
and shuffle the data off.
And now, the worker is unassigned.
It's available for use by another actor.
All of that can happen, as fast as your API
operation or your agent transaction happened.
Again, if another agent-- if another prompt comes in,
we'll start the cycle again.
And eventually, no more messages are received,
and we will shuffle the data off to cloud storage,
and it'll go to sleep for the night.
Looking at the whole thing from the highest level,
a Kubernetes cluster can be a one node cluster on your laptop,
or it can be 200,000 nodes in the cloud.
Each of those nodes can run multiple workers.
Each of those agents are idle, 99.999% of the time.
So you can sue the math and see we're driving up
to those billions of numbers.
Agent Substrate is an open source project.
It is still pre-production grade,
but we're working really hard to get it out into a workable state
by the end of this fall.
And come take a look at it, if you're interested in it.
Take a look at what we've done.
Bring us your feedback.
The most useful thing that we can get from people

We'd love to hear from you.
